brief.head: No face, no brand
brief.text: Perun sells no brand and no cre­den­tials, only the qual­ity of his ar­gu­ment, Ajay Shah said. He called him “the re­pu­di­a­tion of cre­den­tial­ism”[[x11]]. {031-C01}

brief.head: Young nation, old army
brief.text: US Marines av­er­age 21 to 25 years old, Amit Varma said, re­lay­ing Perun; India’s army av­er­ages 32 to 34, be­cause sol­dier­ing is treated as a ca­reer. {031-C10}

brief.head: Uber for artillery
brief.text: When the war began, Ukrainians built an Uber for ar­tillery[[x1]], Amit Varma re­called. Small, em­pow­ered, even sub­ver­sive teams like that, Ajay Shah said, are what armies need. {031-J19}

brief.head: Four wars, no passport
brief.text: France and Germany killed each other[[x4]] from the Napoleonic Wars to 1945, Ajay Shah said. Now peo­ple live in France and drive to work in Germany, show­ing no pass­port. {031-S10}

brief.head: Sukhoi surplus
brief.text: A tid­bit from Perun’s video, as Amit Varma re­layed it: there are more Sukhoi-30s fly­ing over India than over Russia. {#sukhoi}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on what ails India’s military
lead.head: Brains wanted at the front

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 31

body: Ajay Shah set Amit Varma some home­work: a YouTube video on Indian de­fence by Perun, a pseudony­mous econ­o­mist who talks over PowerPoint slides. Varma, who has done sev­eral episodes on the sub­ject, could not find a sin­gle el­e­men­tary error. {031-S02}

The video be­came the launch pad for a long con­ver­sa­tion about what is wrong with India’s armed forces and how to fix it. Shah’s an­swer, again and again, was that a mod­ern mil­i­tary runs on brains.
“Wars are won by think­ing, by clev­er­ness, by cre­ativ­ity, by flex­i­bil­ity, by team­work,” he said.

The macho image of the army, all blood-curdling screams, is a re­cent pop­ulist turn, he ar­gued. The army of Sam Manekshaw, Y. B. Chavan and Indira Gandhi in 1971 was quiet, clin­i­cal and pro­fes­sional.
## Where the money goes

Varma re­layed Perun’s num­bers. The United States spends about ten times as much as India on de­fence, and China about five times. Of India’s bud­get, 53 per cent goes on salaries and pen­sions. {031-C09}

Shah stepped back to first prin­ci­ples. Strategy, he said, has three steps: list the threats, de­sign a force that meets them cost-efficiently, and move to­wards it step by step from where you are. {031-C03}
India’s of­fi­cials rarely think that far ahead. They “play for their time on the watch”, he said: a per­son pro­moted at 59 plays for one year.

Nor is the trou­ble unique to de­fence. Hiring, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing and checks on co­er­cive power break down in health and fi­nance too, Shah said, and spe­cial­ists in their silos never see it.
## The pre­scrip­tion

Shah’s reme­dies began out­side the bar­racks. Diplomacy is the outer layer, he said, and war is what hap­pens when it fails. A coun­try that opens with “strate­gic au­ton­omy”, he ar­gued, has taken its do­mes­tic pol­icy off the ne­go­ti­at­ing table. {031-C07}

Only the United States, he said, can build fron­tier weapons alone at a sen­si­ble cost. India’s at­tempts, the Arjun tank and the Light Combat Aircraft, show what going it alone pro­duces: equip­ment that ar­rives 20 years late.

A poor coun­try should aim one notch be­hind the fron­tier, buy fewer types of equip­ment, and get unit costs down through scale. And it should hire for brain­power, be­cause fit­ness can be trained and brains can­not.
His bold­est idea was a new army be­side the old: small for­ma­tions of about a thou­sand peo­ple with mod­ern man­u­als, woven into the Air Force and Navy, while the old army slowly shrinks.
## The long game
Varma’s thoughts, he said, were “all pes­simistic”: bad in­cen­tives, or­gan­i­sa­tions too os­si­fied to change, and too lit­tle in­tel­lec­tual ca­pac­ity in the state.
Shah added a darker one. Defeat used to force re­form: the loss to China in 1962 led to army re­forms that paid off in 1965 and 1971.
Nuclear de­ter­rence has largely ended such wars be­tween India, China and Pakistan, he said, so weak­nesses may be pil­ing up un­seen. {031-C14}

Yet Shah called him­self fun­da­men­tally op­ti­mistic. For the first time, he said, India is build­ing a lit­er­a­ture, and a new gen­er­a­tion of peo­ple who un­der­stand law, pub­lic ad­min­is­tra­tion and state ca­pac­ity.
Varma had a re­join­der. “Both of us are play­ing a long game,” he said, “but as your hero John Maynard Keynes once said, in the long run, we are all dead.”

second.label: Army and society
second.head: Corps values
second.deck: Ajay Shah on how German veterans fed Nazism, and the road Nehru chose

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Free Corps and the brownshirts

body: After the First World War, Ajay Shah said, German vet­er­ans came back into an in­for­mal or­gan­i­sa­tion[[x13]] called the Free Corps. It be­came home to toxic right-wing na­tion­al­ism: strong­man val­ues, in­tol­er­ance and a will­ing­ness to take to the streets. {#freecorps}[[x14]]

That was the raw ma­te­rial around which the Nazi Party was built, and many brown­shirts came from the Free Corps. Hitler’s so­ci­ety then fed back into a mil­i­tary project to con­quer the whole world. It worked out very badly for Germany.

India, Shah ar­gued, took the other road: keep­ing the army in its bar­racks, pro­fes­sional and out of pol­i­tics, was one of Nehru’s great achieve­ments. {031-S08} Amit Varma pointed to Pakistan, where the mil­i­tary came to dom­i­nate so­ci­ety.

quote.text: It is one of the great achieve­ments of Nehru that the in­sti­tu­tional ar­range­ments were made to keep the army in their bar­racks

third.head: Chess, poker, then biceps

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the army’s recruitment exam

body: Ajay Shah gets very de­pressed by news­pa­per re­ports on how the Indian mil­i­tary hires. Thousands of young men gather at one vil­lage and run 15 kilo­me­tres, and roughly the fastest one per cent are short­listed. {031-S12}
“You could take al­most any per­son and train them to mil­i­tary lev­els of fit­ness,” he said. “You can­not take al­most any per­son and train them to mil­i­tary level of brain power.” {031-C11}

He wants “Vaishnav lev­els of brain power in the mil­i­tary”, nam­ing the episode’s cam­era­man, Vaishnav Vyas. “He’s a wimp, he doesn’t have any bi­ceps,” Shah said. “Adding bi­ceps is triv­ial.” {031-J07}

Paper one of his re­cruit­ment exam: an Elo rat­ing on chess.com. Paper two: poker, be­cause in mil­i­tary af­fairs the board is not vis­i­ble. Ukraine’s army, he added, is 10 per cent women, who make great snipers[[x15]]. {#women}

box.title: Who is Perun?
box.text: Perun is a pseudony­mous econ­o­mist on YouTube whose videos are PowerPoint slides crammed with words, with him talk­ing over them. Amit Varma has never seen him on cam­era. He has about half a mil­lion sub­scribers, and many videos pass a mil­lion views. {#subs}

sections.label: Perun’s diagnosis
sections.head: Four horsemen of procurement
sections.caption: Perun’s case against Indian defence
body: Perun’s start­ing point, as Amit Varma sum­marised it, is that India is not tech­no­log­i­cally back­ward. It ran the Chandrayaan mis­sion for a frac­tion of what other space pro­grammes cost, and it is a nu­clear power. Its armed forces are an­other story.

India did not have to build an army from scratch. It in­her­ited its share of the British Indian Army. Then, as Varma re­layed Perun’s dry hu­mour, “the guns im­me­di­ately turned at each other.” {031-J04}
Asked whose side India is on, es­pe­cially over the Russia-Ukraine war, Perun has a ready an­swer: “India is on India’s side.”
## A beast with old weapons
The Navy and the Air Force, Varma said, are rel­a­tively ad­vanced and evolv­ing quickly. The army is 1.2 mil­lion peo­ple. {#army} It is, he said, “a beast with re­ally old weaponry”.

The money goes on peo­ple. Pensions took 12 per cent of the bud­get in 2008 and take 23 per cent now. Of roughly $47 bil­lion in 2023, only about $3.7 bil­lion went on mod­ernising the force, though Varma warned that some fig­ures might be slightly off. {031-C09}

~ The Agnipath scheme tried to change this, start­ing ev­ery­one on a five-year con­tract. {#agnipath} Those not kept on got a one-time tax-free sev­er­ance in­stead of pen­sions, and the scheme set off protests across the coun­try, be­cause Indians think of the army as a job for life.

quote.text: Fifty-three per­cent of that goes into salaries and pen­sions, of which pen­sions alone ac­count for 23%.

sections.label: Strategy
sections.head: First, list the threats
sections.caption: the three steps of military strategy
body: Ajay Shah set out mil­i­tary strat­egy in three steps. First, write down the threats, which change: China’s econ­omy is now five times the size of India’s. Second, de­sign a force that meets those threats cost-efficiently. Third, move to­wards it.

He wanted “cost ef­fi­cient” in bold: with in­fi­nite ar­tillery you can win every bat­tle, but no­body has it. India spends about 2.5 per cent of GDP on its mil­i­tary, per­haps half a per cent on equip­ment. {#gdp}

Weapons last about 20 years, so re­plac­ing ev­ery­thing at once is out of reach: “nobody’s going to give you that money.” Instead, re-engineer old T-72 and T-90 tanks[[x8]] with new weapons and elec­tron­ics. {031-C03}
## Playing for one year

Amit Varma raised the MiG-21, an air­craft of the 1960s that India should have stopped using 30 years ago. Search for MiG-21 crashes, he said, and you find ex­pe­ri­enced pi­lots dying in them. {031-S04}

Shah traced it to a fail­ure across Indian gov­ern­ment: the in­abil­ity to think strate­gi­cally. Officials plan for their own ten­ure, he said; pro­moted at 59, they play for one year. {031-C04} In Britain, the US and Germany, se­cu­rity com­mu­ni­ties out­last elec­tions and own the 25-year view.

~ Under Narasimha Rao, Vajpayee and Jaswant Singh, after the Soviet Union col­lapsed, India began to re­think its align­ments. Shah judges the ef­fort in­com­plete: a pro-Soviet, pro-Russian strain of think­ing per­sists.

quote.text: Identify your threats, dream of what is an ap­pro­pri­ate force de­sign, and then do that in­cre­men­tal process of evo­lu­tion given where you are

sections.label: Foundations
sections.head: The same plumbing, everywhere
sections.caption: the four foundational processes
body: A health-expert friend of Ajay Shah’s be­lieved for years that Indian health­care worked badly be­cause econ­o­mists kept the best peo­ple in fi­nance. It took him years to per­suade her that fi­nance has huge prob­lems too. {031-S07}

The same fail­ures, Shah said, run through health, fi­nance, de­fence, in­tel­li­gence and mon­e­tary pol­icy. {031-C05} In *In Service of the Republic*, he and Vijay Kelkar call them foun­da­tional pro­cesses: HR, gov­ern­ment con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing and fi­nance, and checks and bal­ances on co­er­cive power.

Specialists miss this be­cause they stay in their silos, and in health they nar­row fur­ther, to polio or HIV. They also treat the plumb­ing as be­yond their pay grade. A mil­i­tary of­fi­cer can­not change the General Financial Rules that gov­ern con­tract­ing.
## Two jobs, done well

Early European states, Shah said, did only two things: raise taxes and wage wars[[x7]]. {031-C06} They ran no ord­nance fac­to­ries. Arms came from pri­vate ven­dors and mer­ce­nar­ies, who even sold arms to Indian kings, so states had to learn to con­tract.

India did it up­side down. Among the poor­est and least ca­pa­ble states in the world, it ex­panded, “in a so­cial­ist frenzy”, into al­most ev­ery­thing, and now does it all at small scale and badly.
~ Amit Varma drew the les­son in the show’s name. Everything is ev­ery­thing, he said: never let your vi­sion get so com­part­men­talised that you miss the broader prin­ci­ples.

quote.text: So this ver­ti­cal­iza­tion, the com­part­men­tal­iza­tion, the dis­ci­plinary em­pha­sis is the source of dif­fi­culty in think­ing about Indian pub­lic pol­icy.

sections.label: Diplomacy first
sections.head: The big stick, used sparingly
sections.caption: diplomacy as defence’s outer layer
body: Amit Varma began with the mil­i­tary the­o­rist Clausewitz, “war is pol­i­tics by other means”, and added a twist: “which means if you’re doing pol­i­tics well, you don’t need the war.” {031-J16}

Ajay Shah took up the theme. Military power is the big stick a coun­try must have and should use as lit­tle as pos­si­ble, be­cause it is very ex­pen­sive and be­cause killing peo­ple is al­ways morally wrong. When war comes, he said, diplo­macy has failed, as it did be­fore the First World War and be­fore Putin in­vaded Ukraine.

In 1947 India in­her­ited a first-rate mil­i­tary: many of its of­fi­cers had trained at Sandhurst. {#sandhurst} It in­her­ited no for­eign-policy ca­pa­bil­ity, and its diplo­mats, Shah said, still make speeches and ne­go­ti­ate noth­ing.
## Dancing alone

Diplomacy means states chang­ing their do­mes­tic poli­cies to suit each other. Open with “strate­gic au­ton­omy”, Shah said, and you de­clare yours off the table: “then very well, go dance alone.” {031-C07}

Treaties and coali­tions let coun­tries in­sure one an­other, which brings down de­fence costs. Taking on China alone, whose econ­omy out­weighs India’s much as Russia’s out­weighs Ukraine’s, would be very ex­pen­sive.

~ Shah even re­cast 1971. Indians blame the United States for back­ing Pakistan, he said, but that align­ment was a fail­ure of Indian for­eign pol­icy, and Bangladesh might have bro­ken free with­out it. {031-S11}

quote.text: Killing less peo­ple is a very high virtue.

sections.label: Self-reliance
sections.head: Twenty years too late
sections.caption: why India cannot build alone
body: Ajay Shah can date the Light Combat Aircraft by his own ed­u­ca­tion. When he started col­lege in 1983, he ben­e­fited greatly from a com­pu­ta­tional fluid dy­nam­ics lab funded as part of the LCA project. {031-S05}

Build fron­tier equip­ment alone, he said, and you can spend decades on it, only to find the world has moved on. Of the Arjun tank and the LCA he said: “It’ll come 20 years late, but 20 years late it’ll be too late.”

Only one coun­try builds such sys­tems alone at a sen­si­ble cost: the United States. {031-C08} It has the deep­est pri­vate ecosys­tem of de­fence re­search[[x9]], funded through DARPA and oth­ers. It builds thou­sands of fight­ers, not hun­dreds. {#thousands} And it does not prac­tise self-reliance: its con­tracts flow to Japan, Israel and Europe.
## Who sells the laser?

Everyone else works in part­ner­ship: Germany with Britain on a fighter, Korea with Poland, Japan with a whole array of coun­tries. Supply chains also run through for­eign pol­icy. If a tank’s laser range finder comes from Sweden, Shah said, being prickly with Sweden puts it at risk.
~ He was also cool on India’s tech­ni­cal prow­ess. Most of the soft­ware done in India, he said, is pretty basic, and its en­gi­neer­ing ca­pa­bil­i­ties are rel­a­tively lim­ited.

quote.text: There is only one coun­try that is able to do iso­lated de­vel­op­ment of global state of the art sys­tems at a half sen­si­ble cost.

sections.label: Defence economics
sections.head: Buy B-grade, buy in bulk
sections.caption: buying one notch behind the frontier
body: A poor coun­try, Ajay Shah said, should aim one notch be­hind the global fron­tier. “I will not buy an F-35. I will buy a B-grade,” he said, and he would pass on the Abrams and Leopard tanks too.
Counting equip­ment mis­leads, he ar­gued, like judg­ing a chess po­si­tion by adding up the pieces. In 1967 the Arabs vastly out­gunned Israel, and Israel won the Six-Day War. {#israel}

Then comes scale[[x16]]: fewer types of equip­ment, in­te­gra­tion into global sup­ply chains, ex­ports. A mix of Rafales, MiG-21s and Sukhois is “con­fused”, he said. “The core in­sight of the mil­i­tary in­dus­trial com­plex of the de­fence in­dus­trial base is scale.” {031-C12}
## A clean slate

Amit Varma doubted that the army could ever be cut down po­lit­i­cally. Shah was un­moved: “This is a coun­try where cus­toms du­ties went from three fifty per­cent to fif­teen per­cent. Anything is pos­si­ble.” {031-J09}

Merging the Navy and Air Force into the­atre com­mands now, he feared, would smother their bet­ter cul­ture. Instead, copy Russia’s bat­tal­ion tac­ti­cal groups and start afresh, with mod­ern man­u­als and pro­cesses, while the old army is phased out like an old pen­sion sys­tem. {031-C13}
~ China’s PLA, he noted, once took in agri­cul­tural sur­plus labour much as India’s army does, then cut about half its per­son­nel. {#pla}

quote.text: It’s a bad work­man who blames his tools.

So there is this feed­back loop that you need to fail, and then enough peo­ple get kicked into ac­tion to un­der­take those dif­fi­cult trans­for­ma­tions. And this is a re­cur­ring theme all across the world of pub­lic pol­icy.

p3.title: War stories
p3.deck: Four tales the hosts told, of procurement, pensions, tanks and the bomb

stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells Perun’s parable of Indian defence buying
stories.head: A township on a room’s budget
body: Imagine you are a for­eign de­fence firm, Amit Varma said, and India comes to you with an order. {#township} He was retelling Perun’s case against Indian de­fence pro­cure­ment in a metaphor of his own, con­ced­ing that Perun had prob­a­bly put it bet­ter.
India gives you the bud­get for a sin­gle room. With it, you must build a super-advanced town­ship, and make it fly to space.

There are con­di­tions. You must work with an Indian part­ner and own only 49 per cent. You must trans­fer all your tech­nol­ogy and know-how. If any­thing goes wrong, you bear 100 per cent of the blame.
And while all this is hap­pen­ing, the re­quire­ments may keep chang­ing, “be­cause some­body will think of some­thing”.

Perun names four horse­men of the de­fence pro­cure­ment apoc­a­lypse[[x10]]: bud­gets, re­quire­ments, de­mands for in­di­geni­sa­tion and bu­reau­cratic pro­ce­dure. The re­quire­ments, a for­mer de­fence min­is­ter said, ac­cord­ing to Perun’s video, read like some­thing “straight out of a Marvel Comics su­per­hero movie”. {031-J05}

Perun’s sum­mary, as Varma re­layed it: the army asks for tech­nol­ogy for 2030 and is told it can have tech­nol­ogy from 2010. It re­fuses. “And we are still stuck with tech­nol­ogy from 1940.” {031-S03}
This, as Perun says in the video, calls for a slow clap. It is, Varma added, a re­mark­ably bad sit­u­a­tion.
~ Later in the episode, Varma said Perun was hardly ex­ag­ger­at­ing. India still has MiG-21s fly­ing over­head, he said, “and crash­ing, mind you”.
stories.why: When bud­gets are tiny, spec­i­fi­ca­tions fan­tas­ti­cal, in­di­geni­sa­tion forced and pro­ce­dures tan­gled, the best ven­dors walk away. The buyer is left with the old­est equip­ment of all, the very op­po­site of what the army asked for.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the township that must fly to space

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a pension reform agreed, then forgotten
stories.head: The pension deal that went AWOL
body: Early in the life of the National Pension System, S. Narayan of the Finance Ministry sent Ajay Shah to hold care­ful meet­ings with the Army, Navy and Air Force on bring­ing the NPS to the mil­i­tary. {#deputed} The se­nior lead­er­ship of all three agreed, orally. Shah did those ne­go­ti­a­tions him­self.

Then the UPA came to power in 2004. The CPI(M) blocked the NPS[[x6]] for years, pen­sions moved, wrongly in Shah’s view, from the Department of Economic Affairs to the Department of Financial Services, and the in­sti­tu­tional mem­ory was lost[[x5]].
By the time the NPS rolled out, the mil­i­tary con­nec­tion was gone. “And today we are hold­ing the night­mare of OROP,” Shah said. “It’s the exact op­po­site of where we had begun.” {031-S06}
~ It was, he said, an ex­am­ple of dis­ci­plinary bound­aries in­ter­rupt­ing the flow of knowl­edge.
stories.why: Reform agree­ments can qui­etly evap­o­rate through changes of gov­ern­ment and bu­reau­cratic reshuf­fles. Here the re­sult was One Rank One Pension, and pen­sions that now swal­low so much of India’s de­fence bud­get.
stories.postscript: Pensions take 23 per cent of the de­fence bud­get, up from 12 per cent in 2008, by Perun’s fig­ures as Varma re­layed them.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the military pension deal that vanished

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on buying one notch below the best
stories.head: Poles apart from self-reliance
body: Poland ex­pects to be next if Ukraine falls, Ajay Shah said, and wants thou­sands of tanks ready for a Russian in­va­sion. {031-S13}

It did not buy the German Leopard or the American Abrams. It bought a very good South Korean tank, a lit­tle be­hind those two, which fits the Polish bud­get. Then it signed deep con­tracts with the Koreans: part­ner­ing in re­search and man­u­fac­tur­ing, tak­ing eq­uity, and earn­ing roy­al­ties on fu­ture sales of those tanks all over the world.
“They didn’t say self-reliance,” Shah said. “They said, let’s be prag­matic.”
~ Korean car­mak­ers al­ready build cars in India, he noted. Korean tank-makers should think of doing the same, be­cause it is cheaper, but India would then have to play for the world mar­ket.
stories.why: A coun­try with lim­ited money does bet­ter to buy one notch below the fron­tier, at scale and through part­ner­ships, than to chase the best equip­ment or self-reliance. India, Shah ar­gued, is such a coun­try. {031-C12}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Poland’s Korean tank

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a handover between prime ministers
stories.head: The material is ready
body: After Narasimha Rao died, Amit Varma said, Atal Bihari Vajpayee told a story about 1996, when Rao handed power to him. Varma counts them as India’s two finest prime min­is­ters.
Rao told him: “Saamagri taiyaar hai[[x2]].” The ma­te­rial is ready; the nu­clear tests can be car­ried out.

Rao had not car­ried out the tests him­self, Varma said, be­cause elec­tions had brought in a new gov­ern­ment, and as a mat­ter of cour­tesy he left them to it. {031-S09} “We are lucky that they had that shared vi­sion that they did.”

~ Manmohan Singh car­ried the turn away from the Soviet Union on. In UPA-1 he pushed the nu­clear deal with the US[[x3]] de­spite the Left, even in his own party, and was ready to stop being prime min­is­ter over it.
stories.why: Strategic shifts sur­vive changes of gov­ern­ment when lead­ers across par­ties share a vi­sion. Ajay Shah’s caveat: the re­align­ment came from the top, from Rao, Vajpayee, Jaswant Singh and Manmohan Singh, not from the bu­reau­cracy, and stayed in­com­plete. {#fromthetop}

overheard.text: Watch all our pre­vi­ous videos, watch Perun’s video, just watch videos all day, right? The world is going to hell. Just watch videos.
overheard.who: Amit Varma, signing off the episode

quiz.q: What does Perun say when asked whose side India is on in the Russia-Ukraine war?
quiz.a: “India is on India’s side”, as Amit Varma re­layed Perun’s dry hu­mour.

quiz.q: What, by Perun’s count, are the four horsemen of the defence procurement apocalypse?
quiz.a: Low bud­gets, crazy re­quire­ments, de­mands for in­di­geni­sa­tion, and bu­reau­cratic pro­ce­dure, as Varma re­layed them.

quiz.q: Which two exams would Ajay Shah set for recruits to the Indian Army?
quiz.a: A chess.com Elo rat­ing, then poker, be­cause on a bat­tle­field the board is hid­den.

quiz.q: What did Narasimha Rao tell Vajpayee when he handed over power in 1996?
quiz.a: “Saamagri taiyaar hai”: the ma­te­rial is ready, the nu­clear tests can go ahead.

quiz.q: Which tank did Poland choose to prepare for a possible Russian invasion, and why?
quiz.a: A very good South Korean tank, a notch below the best, that fits its bud­get.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, has the old loop of reform through defeat stopped working?
quiz.a: Nuclear de­ter­rence be­tween India, China and Pakistan has largely stopped the wars that ex­posed fail­ures.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 31. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Carl von Clausewitz (Wilhelm Wach, public domain); P. V. Narasimha Rao (Christian Lambiotte - European Commission, CC BY 4.0); Atal Bihari Vajpayee (Government of India, GODL-India); Victor Davis Hanson (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Michael Crichton (Jon Chase photo/Harvard News Office, CC BY-SA 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Perun (YouTube channel)
shelf.creator: Perun
shelf.why: Perun is a model sense-maker.

shelf.title: Indian Defence Strategy: Forces, Potential and Procurement Disasters
shelf.creator: Perun
shelf.why: It is de­tailed and ac­cu­rate on the Indian de­fence in­dus­try, with no el­e­men­tary er­rors, and Amit found it bet­ter in­formed than many peo­ple whose job is to know this.

shelf.title: Army and Nation
shelf.creator: Steven I Wilkinson
shelf.why: It is a his­tory of how the Indian Army evolved, in­clud­ing the de­bates in the 40s, 50s and 60s over what role it should play in so­ci­ety.

shelf.title: Strategy: A History
shelf.creator: Lawrence Freedman
shelf.why: Amit calls it mas­ter­ful and mag­is­te­rial, a book packed with knowl­edge and in­sight that he learned a lot from.

shelf.title: Lawrence Freedman’s Substack newsletter
shelf.creator: Lawrence Freedman
shelf.why: Freedman has been writ­ing pro­lif­i­cally on Substack for the past cou­ple of years, ‘and thank God for that.’

shelf.title: The Second World Wars
shelf.creator: Victor Davis Hanson
shelf.why: It is very hard to write a gen­uinely new book on WWII, and Ajay says Hanson has done it, with deeper ideas, a more meta-level anal­y­sis and im­pli­ca­tions for today’s world.

shelf.title: Carnage and Culture
shelf.creator: Victor Davis Hanson
shelf.why: Ajay calls it ‘a very dis­turb­ing book’ and doesn’t agree with all of it, but thinks ev­ery­body should read it.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Rising to the China Challenge (also linked: Chapter 1)
shelf.creator: Gautam Bambawale, Vijay Kelkar, Raghunath Mashelkar, Ganesh Natarajan, Ajit Ranade & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It ar­gues that India is out­matched by China’s might and must build deep part­ner­ships with other coun­tries.

shelf.title: The Three Globalizations (Episode 17)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s frame­work of three glob­al­i­sa­tions, from the first era with­out cap­i­tal con­trols, when London bond is­sues built Indian rail­ways, to today’s, where ac­cess to the ad­vanced-economy core de­pends on good be­hav­iour in mil­i­tary and for­eign af­fairs.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A five-and-a-half-hour mas­ter­class from Ajay on the war and the deep his­to­ries of Russia and Ukraine, built on a life­time of read­ing and a counter to Russian pro­pa­ganda.

shelf.title: The State of the Ukraine War (Episode 14)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mil­i­tary-strategy anal­y­sis of the war: how it is chang­ing the way wars are fought, Ukrainian in­no­va­tion, and its de­mo­graphic toll on Russia, from deaths to the flight of a mil­lion of its best and bright­est.

shelf.title: ‘Wet Streets Cause Rain’: Michael Crichton explains Gell-Mann Amnesia
shelf.creator: Michael Crichton
shelf.why: Crichton’s ex­pla­na­tion of Gell-Mann Amnesia: we catch the media get­ting our own field wrong, then trust it on ev­ery­thing else.

shelf.title: The Indian Armed Forces (Episode 175 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Lt Gen Prakash Menon
shelf.why: An ear­lier deep con­ver­sa­tion about the Indian Army with Lt Gen Prakash Menon, who gives the army’s side on Kashmir: what is it sup­posed to do if Pakistan sends its peo­ple in?

shelf.title: Keeping India Safe (Episode 219 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Sushant Singh
shelf.why: It gives more back­ground on Indian na­tional se­cu­rity.

shelf.title: 2,374 IAF Crashes. 1,305 Pilots Killed
shelf.creator: Ajai Shukla and Devesh Kapur
shelf.why: It puts num­bers on the human cost of age­ing air­craft and failed plan­ning.

shelf.title: India’s Far From Free Markets (2005, Wall Street Journal)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It is Amit’s early ar­gu­ment that India’s lib­er­al­i­sa­tion was in­com­plete.

shelf.title: The Reformers (Episode 28)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The human story of the peo­ple who worked be­hind the scenes, often for decades and with­out re­ward, to open India up in 1991.

shelf.title: India’s Massive Pensions Crisis (Episode 347 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah and Renuka Sane
shelf.why: Ajay and Renuka Sane on the old ver­sus new pen­sion scheme: a bi­par­ti­san re­form built by a small in­tel­lec­tual com­mu­nity, and how in­sti­tu­tional mem­ory van­ished once that com­mu­nity dis­persed.

shelf.title: Understanding the State, When Should the State Act?, and We Love Vaccines! We Love Freedom! (Episodes 25–27 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: The Geopolitics of the Bangladesh War (Episode 113 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Srinath Raghavan
shelf.why: Amit says the episode has been a ‘gate­way drug’ for many lis­ten­ers, and it gives the diplo­matic back­ground to 1971.

shelf.title: What is the cost of one-rank-one-pension?
shelf.creator: Renuka Sane and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Renuka Sane and Ajay put a cost on the OROP scheme that the hosts blame for crowd­ing out mil­i­tary mod­erni­sa­tion, and pub­lished all their code and as­sump­tions so read­ers can rerun the num­bers.

shelf.title: Public Finance research at XKDR Forum
shelf.creator: XKDR Forum
shelf.why: XKDR Forum’s re­search pro­gramme on pub­lic fi­nance and gov­ern­ment con­tract­ing, stud­ied field by field to draw gen­eral lessons.

shelf.title: An Ode to Perun (and Orry)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It is a writ­ten ver­sion of Amit’s ad­mi­ra­tion for Perun.

laughs.text: Ajay: Perun is ‘not a Harvard MIT New York Times.’ Amit: ‘As far as we know.’

Ajay calls Perun ‘em­bold­en­ing for the bor­ing old fo­gies like you and me, who are the pur­vey­ors of this kind of dreary multi-hour con­tent.’ Amit: ‘Speak for your­self, Ajay Shah. You know, I am not bor­ing and dreary and old, at least com­pared to you.’
Amit’s pun on Y. B. Chavan: ‘Mr. Chavan was a man also given not just to mil­i­tary af­fairs but meta­physics, be­cause he would al­ways be think­ing, why be Chavan?’

Perun’s dry hu­mour, as Amit re­lays it: when India and Pakistan in­her­ited their shares of the British Indian Army, ‘the guns im­me­di­ately turned at each other.’ And when asked whose side India is on, Perun an­swers: ‘India is on India’s side.’
A for­mer de­fence min­is­ter, per Perun’s video, said the army’s weapon re­quire­ments read like some­thing ‘straight out of a Marvel Comics su­per­hero movie.’
Asked for the way out, Ajay an­swers: ‘Intellectualism, ev­ery­thing is ev­ery­thing.’ Amit: ‘As usual, you’re giv­ing glib an­swers to se­ri­ous ques­tions.’

Ajay on the brains a mil­i­tary needs: ‘You want Vaishnav lev­els of brain power in the mil­i­tary. I mean, he’s a wimp, he doesn’t have any bi­ceps. Adding bi­ceps is triv­ial.’ Vaishnav Vyas shot the episode.

When Amit doubts that the army could ever be cut down po­lit­i­cally, Ajay replies: ‘This is a coun­try where cus­toms du­ties went from three fifty per­cent to fif­teen per­cent. Anything is pos­si­ble.’
Amit: ‘It’s so sad that none of us know much about the Indian Navy given the amount of naval gaz­ing we do.’
After Ajay’s op­ti­mistic long view, Amit says: ‘both of us are play­ing a long game, but as your hero John Maynard Keynes once said, in the long run, we are all dead.’
Gell-Mann am­ne­sia: Michael Crichton’s term, named after physi­cist Murray Gell-Mann, for trust­ing a news­pa­per on ev­ery­thing ex­cept the one sub­ject you know it gets wrong.
Clausewitz’s ‘war is pol­i­tics by other means’, with Amit’s twist: ‘which means if you’re doing pol­i­tics well, you don’t need the war.’
Ajay: ‘ever since Joan of Arc, the fa­nat­ics don’t re­ally win wars.’ He con­trasts this with the toxic mas­culin­ity of Telugu and Bollywood films’ por­trayal of the army.
‘Adapt, im­pro­vise, overcome’, the US Marines say­ing Ajay uses to de­scribe the brainy force India needs.
A tid­bit from Perun’s video: there are now more Sukhoi-30s fly­ing over India than over Russia.
